title: Head, Heart and Trust
subject: English
unit: Spring 2: Julius Caesar (Shakespeare): leadership, persuasion and responsibility
source: Written for english/y8 lesson 34 ('Head, Heart and Trust' (teacher-written explanatory article, pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 34: Non-fiction: the psychology of persuasion. Read the whole text, then annotate it: underline the writer's methods and note their effect in the margin.

passage.title: Head, Heart and Trust
paras: More than two thousand years ago, the Greek thinker Aristotle described three ways to persuade. Ethos appeals to trust: we listen to people we believe are honest or expert. Pathos appeals to emotion: a story of suffering can move us more than a page of figures. Logos appeals to reason: facts, statistics and step-by-step arguments.

Skilled persuaders combine all three. A charity appeal might open with a child's story (pathos), quote a doctor (ethos) and finish with the cost of a vaccine (logos). The danger is that the same tools can be used to mislead.

Advertisers know this well. A sports drink advert may show an athlete we admire (ethos), music-free footage of a last-minute victory (pathos) and a claim that the drink 'hydrates 20% faster' (logos). Each appeal sounds convincing on its own, but together they can stop us asking simple questions: faster than what, and who measured it?

Politicians, campaigners and even friends use the same methods. That does not make persuasion wrong. Persuasion is how people change unfair laws, raise money for those in need and convince a friend to stop a dangerous habit. The question is not whether someone is persuading us, but whether they are being honest.

So how can a careful listener protect themselves? First, ask who is speaking and why they might want you to agree. Second, notice your feelings: if a message makes you angry or frightened very quickly, slow down. Third, check the facts: a number without a source is only a number.
Aristotle's three appeals are still everywhere, from playground arguments to election speeches. Learning to spot them does not make us cynical. It makes us free to choose.

questions.q: What is the writer's main viewpoint?
questions.a: Persuasion uses ethos, pathos and logos; it is not wrong in itself, but listeners must check honesty.

questions.q: Find two methods the writer uses and explain the effect of each.
questions.a: Explaining terms with clear definitions; the example of a charity appeal and an advert; numbered advice (First, Second, Third).

questions.q: How does the final paragraph end the argument?
questions.a: It turns knowledge into freedom: 'free to choose'.

questions.q: Retrieve the three appeals with one example each from the article.
questions.a: Ethos: quoting a doctor; pathos: a child's story; logos: the cost of a vaccine.

questions.q: Why does the article end with 'The danger...'?
questions.a: To warn readers that persuasion can mislead, adding a moral note.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, explain how the writer helps readers understand persuasion. Use two methods. Starter: 'The writer explains persuasion by...'
questions.a: Two methods (e.g. the three-part structure, the charity example) with quoted evidence and effects.

questions.q: Extend: which appeal does Cassius rely on most? Justify.
questions.a: Pathos: he stirs Brutus's fear and pride with images like the Colossus.

questions.q: Stretch: how could you protect yourself from misleading persuasion?
questions.a: Check the facts (logos), ask who benefits, notice when emotion is being used to rush you.

questions.q: 'A story of suffering can move us' describes...
questions.a: A) pathos. Emotion is pathos; logic is logos; trust is ethos.

questions.q: Answer the ponder: head or heart?
questions.a: Answers vary, with an example and the appeal named.
